topic: Distress, Urgency, Safety and Warning Signals
summary: There are two states of emergency. Distress (MAYDAY) is grave and imminent danger needing immediate help; urgency (PAN PAN) is a safety concern without immediate danger. Call first on the frequency in use, otherwise 121.5 MHz, and squawk 7700. Visual distress signals are SOS, red flares or a red parachute flare; flashing landing or navigation lights and white flares mean 'I must land but don't need help'; XXX is an urgent safety message. Student pilots say STUDENT. If you stray into a danger area, leave it as fast as possible without descending. Low on fuel and in danger: declare a MAYDAY.

note.file: 13 Distress Urgency Safety and Warning Signals.md

sections: The two states of emergency
Distress: threatened by grave and/or imminent danger, needing immediate assistance. Prefix "MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY".
Urgency: a condition concerning the safety of an aircraft, vehicle or person on board or in sight, not needing immediate assistance. Prefix "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN".
Transmit first on the frequency in use; if you're not in contact with anyone, or get no reply, use 121.5 MHz.
Distress signals
Radio: "MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY", then the message. Example order:
– station addressed ("London Centre", or the unit you are talking to)
– callsign (and type)
– nature of the emergency ("engine has failed")
– intentions ("making a forced landing")
– position, level and heading ("five miles north of the field, three thousand feet descending, heading two eight zero")
– pilot qualification ("student pilot"), not an ICAO requirement but it helps the controller plan
Student pilots add "STUDENT" to their callsign when solo and in an emergency message on any frequency, so instructions are kept simple.
Visual: SOS in Morse (· · · − − − · · ·) by light; a succession of red pyrotechnics at short intervals; a red parachute flare.
Sound: SOS in Morse; a continuous sound from any apparatus.
Urgency signals
An aircraft in difficulties that compel it to land, but not needing immediate help:
– repeated switching on and off of the landing lights
– repeated switching on and off of the navigation lights (distinguishable from normal flashing)
– a succession of white pyrotechnic lights
An aircraft with an urgent message about the safety of a ship, aircraft, vehicle, property or person (on board or in sight):
– Radio: "PAN PAN" ×3, e.g. reporting another aircraft that has force-landed and its occupants
– Visual or sound: XXX in Morse (− · · − ×3)
Exam trap Flashing landing lights or white flares mean "I must land, but don't need help now"; red flares mean distress.
Using the transponder
7700 emergency, 7600 radio failure, 7500 unlawful interference, with Mode C selected.
If you're already squawking a code given by a unit you're talking to, normally keep it.
Danger areas
DACS (Danger Area Crossing Service): a unit can tell you whether a danger area is active and may give a crossing clearance. Marked on the 1:500,000 chart with a prefix symbol.
DAAIS (Danger Area Activity Information Service): tells you whether an area is active, but is not a clearance to cross.
Details: AIP ENR 5, the chart's list of danger areas and Pooley's.
If you inadvertently enter a danger or prohibited area, leave it as quickly as possible without descending, even without a radio instruction.
Low fuel
If the fuel state means you need priority, declare a MAYDAY (ICAO phraseology: "MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY FUEL"), but only if you believe the aircraft is in danger, and make it match the real fuel state.

The book recommends arriving over the destination with enough to approach, go around, fly to an alternate, land there and hold for 45 minutes. For Part-NCO VFR flights the legal final reserve is 30 minutes by day and 45 minutes at night; plan for more.

sum.The two states of emergency: Distress (MAYDAY): grave and imminent danger. Urgency (PAN PAN): a concern, no immediate danger.
sum.Distress signals: MAYDAY ×3 then the message; SOS, red flares or a red parachute flare; a continuous sound.
sum.Urgency signals: Flashing landing or nav lights and white flares: must land, no help needed. XXX or PAN PAN: urgent safety message.
sum.Using the transponder: 7700 emergency, 7600 radio failure, 7500 unlawful interference, with Mode C.
sum.Danger areas: DACS can clear you across; DAAIS only says if an area is active. Strayed in? Leave without descending.
sum.Low fuel: Declare a MAYDAY if the fuel state puts you in danger; Part-NCO reserves are 30 min day, 45 min night.

cards.a: Grave and/or imminent danger, needing immediate assistance.
A safety concern for an aircraft, vehicle or person, not needing immediate assistance.
The frequency in use; 121.5 MHz if not in contact or no reply.
SOS by light, red pyrotechnics at short intervals, a red parachute flare.

cards.q: Flashing landing lights or white flares mean?
cards.a: Difficulties compel me to land, but I don't need immediate help.
An urgent message about the safety of a ship, aircraft, vehicle or person.
So the controller keeps instructions simple.
DACS: crossing service, may give a clearance. DAAIS: activity information only, not a clearance.
Leave as quickly as possible without descending.

quiz.q: The two states of emergency are:
o: Distress and urgency
Mayday and pan pan
Difficulty and urgency
Distress and danger
quiz.why: The states are distress and urgency; MAYDAY and PAN PAN are their radio prefixes, not the states.

quiz.q: A MAYDAY should first be transmitted on:
o: The frequency in use
The nearest MATZ frequency
The London Information frequency
quiz.why: The unit you're talking to can help fastest. Use 121.5 MHz if you're not with anyone or get no reply.

o: Threatened by grave and/or imminent danger and needing immediate assistance
A condition concerning safety that does not need immediate assistance
Any failure of the engine, whether or not a safe landing is possible
Being unsure of your position and needing a steer to an aerodrome
quiz.why: Distress needs immediate assistance; the second option is urgency.

quiz.q: You see an aircraft repeatedly switching its landing lights on and off. It means:
o: It must land but does not need immediate assistance
It is in distress and needs immediate help
It is warning you of a collision
It has an urgent message about another aircraft
quiz.why: Flashing landing or navigation lights (or white flares) are the 'must land, no immediate help' signal. Red flares are distress; XXX is the urgent-message signal.

quiz.q: XXX sent by light in Morse means:
o: An urgent message about the safety of a ship, aircraft, vehicle or person
Distress: grave and imminent danger, and immediate assistance is needed
Radio failure: the aircraft can receive but cannot transmit messages
Land at this aerodrome and await further instructions from ATC
quiz.why: XXX is the urgency signal for an urgent safety message. SOS is distress.

quiz.q: Which of these is a distress signal?
o: A red parachute flare
A succession of white pyrotechnics
Repeated switching of navigation lights
XXX in Morse
quiz.why: Red flares and SOS are distress. White flares and flashing lights are urgency (must land).

o: Danger Area Crossing Service
Danger Area Clearance Service
Danger Area Activity Service
Danger Area Coordination Service
quiz.why: Crossing Service; it may give you a clearance. DAAIS is the Activity Information Service.

quiz.q: You realise you have entered an active danger area. You should:
o: Leave as quickly as possible without descending
Descend below its base as quickly as possible
Orbit where you are and call the controlling unit
Climb above its upper limit, then continue
quiz.why: Leave by the quickest route without descending, even with no radio instruction.

quiz.q: Your fuel state means you will land with less than your final reserve. You should:
o: Declare a MAYDAY to get priority
Call PAN PAN and ask for a direct route
Say nothing until overhead
Squawk 7600
quiz.why: Fuel at or below reserve puts the aircraft in danger: MAYDAY (ICAO: 'MAYDAY FUEL'). 7600 is radio failure.
